title: AlphaHealth pilot weekly economics review & tuning
next_steps: Jordan to send updated batching config and sample traces by 2025-04-11
Customer to run 24h throughput test with new KV cache settings and report token/sec/$ by next sync
Schedule latency-sensitive canary on dedicated pool for 1000 qps
action_items: Jordan Lee - Share per-route token cost calc (sheet) - 2025-04-11
Samir Patel - Provide tuned batching + cache policy JSON and recommended quantization - 2025-04-10

summary: Weekly POC sync focused on unit economics (tokens per second per dollar), caching and batching tradeoffs, and next steps to reduce per-token cost while meeting latency SLOs. Agreed to try more aggressive prefix caching for chat flows and a 50ms batching sweet spot for most routes with exceptions for high-priority low-latency paths.
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining the AlphaHealth weekly sync. Agenda: quick cost recap, tuning updates, and next steps. I'm Jordan from Redwood.
[00:08] Maya Chen: Hi! Quick context — pilot's been running ~10 days, main workload is patient triage chat, avg prompt 280 tokens, responses ~420 tokens — lots of short follow-ups.
[00:25] Samir Patel: Got it. We've been looking at two levers: caching + batching. Quick number: with current config you're at ~0.9 tokens/sec/$ on hosted; with prefix KV cache on we see 1.6 tokens/sec/$ in our small traces.
[00:40] Ravi Gupta: Sorry can you repeat the units — tokens per second per dollar? I think my team was measuring tokens per dollar only.
[00:46] Samir Patel: Right, we normalize throughput (tokens/second) by cost to get tokens/sec/$. Helps compare latency-optimized vs batch-optimized configs.
[00:55] Liam O'Neil: The infra question is — if we enable prefix caching, what’s the memory footprint per session? We worry about our long-tail sessions.
[01:05] Samir Patel: Roughly 12–18 KB per active chat for KV entries with our quantized checkpoints; long-tail can be evicted after 30 min idle. We can tune TTL.
[01:18] Maya Chen: And how does batching affect latency on our 95th pct? Past week we saw p95 jump from 220ms to 460ms when we increased batch windows.
[01:28] Jordan Lee: This is the common tradeoff — batching helps tokens/sec/$ but increases tail latency. For your triage flow we suggested a hybrid: 50ms batching window for standard routes, disable batching for high-priority route that needs sub-300ms p95.
[01:42] Ravi Gupta: Ok makes sense. Can we quantify cost delta if we do hybrid? Our CFO wants a per-1M-token comparison.
[01:50] Samir Patel: Rough delta from our model: hybrid saves ~23% compared to no batching, while full aggressive batching saves ~42% but hits p95 high. So per 1M tokens you'd see about $X -> but I'll share the exact sheet.
[02:05] Sofia Alvarez: From procurement perspective, we also need clarity on data retention — if we enable caching, does that change data residency or logs?
[02:14] Jordan Lee: No, prefix/KV cache is ephemeral and stored in the serving layer; persistent storage policies unchanged. All logs and audit entries still obey your retention policy in the console and KMS controls apply.
[02:27] Ravi Gupta: There was also a question about quantization. Our initial test on int8 caused minor regression on hallucination for clinical entities. Is there a recommended path?
[02:37] Samir Patel: We recommend mixed-precision quantization and running focused evals on your clinical prompt set. For this pilot, try q4_0 for general + spot-check q8 variants on critical prompts. We can roll back if we see regression.
[02:52] Maya Chen: Great — can Redwood run a targeted eval with our 200 clinical prompts and flag regressions?
[02:56] Jordan Lee: Yes, we'll run evals. Ask you to upload the prompt set to the shared drive; Samir will configure the eval harness.
[03:04] (crosstalk)/
[03:10] Samir Patel: Also one technical note: enabling prefix cache increases CPU on the host marginally due to lookups; on dedicated pools CPU headroom should be fine, but on shared hosted quotas may throttle very spiky traffic.
[03:22] Liam O'Neil: That's important — we might prefer a dedicated small pool for peak hours if spikes correlate with clinic opening times.
[03:30] Jordan Lee: We can propose a schedule-based routing policy: hosted for base load, dedicated reserved capacity for peak windows; automatic fallback to smaller model variant if dedicated capacity hits limit.
[03:45] Ravi Gupta: Can you remind us about the fallback model accuracy differences? Our users are sensitive to wrong triage categories.
[03:51] Samir Patel: Fallback model typically quantized smaller architecture; per our tests accuracy delta on your dataset is ~1.8% absolute for triage labels — we'll surface per-intent confusion matrix in the sheet.
[04:05] Maya Chen: Ok. On actionables — sampling: we want a 24h run that simulates realistic traffic with prefix cache enabled and batching window at 50ms. Also measure tokens/sec/$ and p95.
[04:18] Jordan Lee: We'll send the config and a load spec. Also recommend running a second test with 150ms window to compare cost vs p95.
[04:28] Ravi Gupta: For the 1M-token cost estimate, please include both inference and request overheads; our finance team doesn't like surprises.
[04:35] Samir Patel: Agreed — we'll include API request overhead and RBAC/console charges where relevant. Sending the spreadsheet afterwards.
[04:44] Sofia Alvarez: Last question — SLA around dedicated pools? If we commit to reserved capacity what uptime SLA applies?
[04:50] Jordan Lee: Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency targets; we'll include the standard SLA PDF in the share. For pilots we can offer lenient commit terms.
[04:59] Maya Chen: Great. Any blockers from Redwood side?
[05:02] Samir Patel: Need the clinical prompt set and a service account to run benchmarks against your staging VPC. Also need permission to access a small sample of logs to compute per-route token counts.
[05:14] Jordan Lee: I'll follow up with specific IAM roles and a checklist.
[05:18] Maya Chen: Perfect. Thanks all.
[05:20] Jordan Lee: Thanks, we'll sync next week same time. Bye.
